query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the classical EAM reference in thermodynamic integration with a dedicated neural-network interatomic potential (trained on ab initio liquid-state configurations) for near-equimolar multi-component alloys at ~0.9–1.1 Tm will improve liquid-phase sampling and reduce free-energy path errors compared to EAM-based TOR-TILD references.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-principal element (high-entropy) alloys in near-equimolar composition, both solid and liquid, in the temperature window surrounding their melting points (~0.9–1.1 Tm).
generation.intervention: Use an ab initio-trained neural-network potential instead of an EAM potential as the reference in thermodynamic integration, ensuring a high-diversity training set from first-principles snapshots of relevant liquid configurations.
generation.conditions: Perform molecular dynamics from ~0.9–1.1 Tm under ambient pressures for at least two representative quinary (or higher) high-entropy alloy compositions. Maintain consistent system size and sampling times compatible with ab initio-based training data coverage.
generation.structural_mediator: The neural-network reference will capture short-range order in multi-element liquid configurations, broadening the phase space overlap between classical MD references and ab initio data.
generation.mechanism: In contrast to the fixed functional forms of EAM potentials, the flexible high-dimensional form of the neural-network potential encodes complex multi-body interactions that govern local structure in the high-temperature liquid, thereby reducing the mismatch between reference and target thermodynamic paths.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced discrepancies in free-energy calculations relative to ab initio benchmarks, with an expected improvement of a few meV/atom in thermodynamic-integration path consistency compared to EAM-based TOR-TILD references.
generation.baseline: Existing EAM-based references in TOR-TILD simulations of high-entropy alloys at near-melting conditions, which exhibit significant path deviations when integrated against ab initio data.
generation.boundary: Suitable for quinary or higher-order near-equimolar high-entropy alloys with melting points up to ~2000 K. Sufficiently large and diverse ab initio training data is needed for robust neural-network reference potentials.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative gains in free-energy accuracy remain uncertain and may depend on training-set quality and complexity of the composition in question. Transferability beyond tested compositions or temperature windows also remains to be validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Directly compare ab initio thermodynamic integration for each alloy composition with analogous multi-stage integration using the neural-network potential as the classical reference, evaluating both solid and liquid states near Tm.
measurements: Relative free energies in the solid and liquid as determined by both ab initio integration and neural-network-based classical integration.
Systematic comparison of the differences in Gibbs free energy along the integration path between the neural-network-based and EAM-based references.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the neural-network reference yields no significant improvement or introduces larger discrepancies than EAM-based references (e.g., free-energy deviations > a few meV/atom from ab initio), the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

decision.trend: Recent work on multi-principal element alloys with EAM-based molecular dynamics reveals that while EAM can handle near-equimolar compositions at modest temperatures (e.g., for HfNbTaTiZr or AuCoCuNiPt), it struggles to capture liquid-state complexities and the large configurational variability. Studies have shown notable discrepancies in high-temperature diffusion behavior, phase separation, and energy landscape sampling, emphasizing that classical EAM forms cannot span the vast configuration space of liquid high-entropy alloys. Although these EAM-based simulations have advanced understanding of solid-phase or nanoparticle configurations, they do not resolve the liquid’s intricate local ordering or provide accurate free-energy measures. The open challenge remains to reliably align molecular dynamics references with ab initio data in the high-temperature liquid region, where short-range ordering and multi-body interactions are pronounced.
decision.unsolved: EAM references still poorly sample the dynamic, high-dimensional configuration space of multicomponent liquids near their melting points, causing inaccurate free-energy evaluations and large path mismatches compared to ab initio methods.
decision.lever: Train a neural-network-based interatomic potential (e.g., a deep neural network potential) for the high-temperature liquid regime using ab initio configurations spanning the relevant composition–temperature range (~0.9–1.1 Tm) to ensure adequate sampling of local atomic environments. Validate the ML potential by comparing free energies from thermodynamic integration against direct ab initio results for at least two representative high-entropy compositions near their melting points.
decision.why: Machine-learning potentials can systematically incorporate multi-element ab initio data from liquid configurations, thereby improving overlap with target phase space and reducing thermodynamic-integration path mismatch. Prior success modeling smaller binary or single-element melts suggests general feasibility, provided sufficient ab initio training data. A direct free-energy comparison with a benchmark ab initio integration route (e.g., constrained ab initio molecular dynamics) at multiple temperatures would confirm or falsify the improved accuracy in capturing liquid-phase configurational complexity.
